reactions.description: Sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, forming an ionic bond. This is the reaction that makes table salt.
Two hydrogen atoms share electrons with one oxygen atom to form water, the most important molecule for life.
Two hydrogen atoms share their single electrons in a covalent bond, forming stable hydrogen gas.
Carbon forms two double bonds with oxygen, releasing energy. This is what powers every fire and every breath you exhale.
Iron slowly transfers electrons to oxygen in the presence of moisture, forming rust over days or years.
Copper gives electrons to oxygen when heated, forming the black copper oxide seen on tarnished copper.
Magnesium burns so intensely it gives two electrons to oxygen instantly, releasing brilliant white light.
Potassium, like sodium, readily gives its outermost electron to chlorine to form a stable ionic salt.
Calcium gives two electrons to oxygen, forming quicklime. Used in construction for thousands of years.
Aluminum instantly forms a thin Al₂O₃ coating in air, which is why aluminum doesn't rust like iron.
One nitrogen shares electrons with three hydrogens. Ammonia is the basis of nearly all fertilizers.
Carbon shares electrons with four hydrogens. Methane is the main component of natural gas and a powerful greenhouse gas.
Hydrogen and chlorine share electrons unevenly — chlorine's pull makes HCl a strong acid.
Lithium transfers its single valence electron to oxygen, forming a white ionic solid.
Sulfur forms double bonds with two oxygen atoms. SO₂ from volcanoes and coal burning causes acid rain.
This unusual molecule has an unpaired electron. It controls blood pressure in your body and is a major air pollutant.
Iron and sulfur react at high temperatures to form pyrite — often mistaken for gold by early prospectors.
Copper reacts with sulfur to form dark copper sulfide, the mineral basis of many copper ores.
Phosphorus burns intensely in air, reacting with oxygen. P₂O₅ is a powerful desiccant.
Silicon forms covalent bonds with oxygen, creating the quartz in sand and the glass in your phone screen.
Zinc transfers electrons to sulfur. ZnS glows under UV light and was used in early TV and radar screens.
Silver slowly reacts with sulfur compounds in air to form black Ag₂S — the tarnish on silver jewelry.
Barium reacts violently with oxygen; BaO reacts with water to form strongly alkaline barium hydroxide.
Titanium transfers electrons to oxygen to form brilliant white TiO₂ — the white pigment in paint and sunscreen.
Manganese forms MnO₂, the active material in alkaline batteries that powers your remote controls.
Lead and sulfur form galena, the most important lead ore. It was used as eyeliner in ancient Egypt.
Potassium reacts explosively with oxygen. Even a small piece of potassium ignites instantly in air.
Calcium and carbon bond at very high temperatures. CaC₂ reacts with water to produce acetylene, used in welding.
Helium has a completely full outer electron shell. It forms no chemical bonds with anything — not even itself.
Gold is so unreactive it has been found as pure metal since ancient times. Its filled d-orbitals resist sharing electrons.
